title: Family emergency plan and meeting points
context: A family emergency plan says how you will reach each other, where you will meet near home and out of the neighborhood, and who an out-of-area contact is. Also called family plan, where do we meet, meeting place, family emergency card. Look for a meeting spot near home and one farther away; an out-of-area contact everyone knows. Write the plan down, give every family member a card, and practice it twice a year.

title: What to teach a child about being lost in the woods
context: A child who is lost should stay in one place, hug a tree, make noise, and answer when called; searchers find children who stay put far faster. Also called kid lost in woods, hug a tree, child lost hiking, teach kids if lost. Look for a whistle on the child's jacket; bright clothing. Teach: stop, hug a tree, blow the whistle three times, stay put, and answer anyone calling your name. Practice it as a game.

title: How a child calls 911
context: Children can call 911 from any phone, even a locked one, and should say what happened, where they are, and stay on the line. Also called teach kids to call 911, child emergency call, what to say to 911. Look for how to reach emergency call on your phone's lock screen; the child knows their address. Teach your address, how to place an emergency call on a locked phone, and to answer the dispatcher's questions and stay on the line.

title: Keeping children warm and spotting cold stress in infants
context: Children lose heat faster than adults; an infant with hypothermia can have bright red, cold skin and very low energy. Also called baby hypothermia, infant cold, keeping kids warm, child too cold. Look for bright red, cold skin in a baby; a quiet, floppy, or very sleepy child. Dress children in one more layer than adults, cover the head, change wet clothes at once, and warm a cold child against your body in a dry blanket.

title: Dehydration and fever in a child
context: Children dehydrate quickly with vomiting, diarrhea, heat, or fever; a dry mouth, few wet diapers, no tears, and unusual sleepiness are warning signs. Also called child dehydrated, kid fever, baby dehydration signs, when to take child to doctor. Look for fewer wet diapers or no urine for many hours; no tears when crying, a dry mouth, sunken eyes. Give small, frequent sips of fluid or oral rehydration solution, keep the child cool, and watch urine and alertness.

title: Kids outdoors: ticks, poison ivy, water, and firearms
context: A few short rules prevent most outdoor harm to children: check for ticks, avoid leaves of three, stay within reach near water, and never touch a gun. Also called kids safety outdoors, children and guns, kids near water, kids ticks. Look for a tick check after every outing; a life jacket on near water. Teach: if you see a gun, don't touch, leave, tell an adult. Keep children within arm's reach near water and do a full tick check at night.

title: Infant formula when the water is unsafe
context: When tap water is unsafe, infant formula should be ready-to-feed, or mixed with bottled water or water that was boiled and cooled. Also called baby formula water, boil water notice baby, formula during outage. Look for a boil-water notice; flooding near the well. Use ready-to-feed formula when you can; otherwise use bottled water or water brought to a rolling boil for one minute and cooled. Clean bottles in safe water.

title: A child left in a vehicle is an emergency
context: A closed car heats up fast even on a mild day and can kill a child within minutes; in winter, a running car can fill with exhaust. Also called child left in car, kid in hot car, baby in car heat. Look for a child alone in a car; a sweaty, red, or unresponsive child. If you see a child alone in a hot car, call 911 at once and follow the dispatcher's directions. Make a habit of checking the back seat every time you leave the car.

title: Pet kit, pet evacuation, and pet poisoning
context: Pets need their own emergency kit and a plan for where they can stay, because many shelters only take service animals. Also called pet emergency kit, evacuate with pets, dog ate something toxic, pet poison. Look for food, water, medicines, leash, carrier, and records; a list of pet-friendly hotels or friends. Pack a pet kit, plan pet-friendly places to stay, and take pets with you if you evacuate.

title: Talking to children during an emergency
context: Children take their cue from adults; calm, simple, honest words and a job to do help them feel safer. Also called kids scared storm, calm a child, explain disaster to kids, child anxiety emergency. Look for a child clinging, crying, or very quiet; questions repeated many times. Get down to their level, say what is happening in a few words, tell them what you are doing to keep them safe, and give them a small task.

title: Reuniting a family after a storm or evacuation
context: After a disaster, families reunite fastest when everyone knows the meeting places and the out-of-area contact ahead of time. Also called find family after disaster, separated from family, reunification. Look for the planned meeting spot; an out-of-area contact who relays messages. Go to the planned meeting place, text the out-of-area contact, and register with official shelters or reunification services.

title: School or daycare pickup when phones or roads fail
context: A pickup plan names who can collect each child, how the school will reach you, and what happens if roads or phones are down. Also called school emergency pickup, who picks up the kids, school lockdown parent. Look for the school's emergency and release policy; backup adults on the authorized pickup list. Learn the school's plan, add backup adults to the pickup list, and tell children who may collect them.

title: Child carriers and trail safety with little ones
context: Hiking with a baby or toddler needs a carrier that fits both of you, extra warmth and sun protection for the child, and short, flexible plans. Also called hiking with a baby, child carrier backpack, toddler on trail. Look for the child's face, hands, and feet staying warm or shaded; the carrier's weight limit. Check the child often, dress them warmer than you since they are not moving, take breaks, and avoid steep or icy ground.

title: Shared kit: who carries the meds and the inhaler
context: In a group, life-saving medicines such as an epinephrine auto-injector or an inhaler must stay with the person who needs them, with a backup someone else knows about. Also called who carries epipen, family medicines trip, inhaler on hike. Look for an epinephrine auto-injector with the allergic person; a spare inhaler with another adult. Decide before leaving who carries what, show others where it is, and keep medicines protected from heat and freezing.

title: Pets in a power outage, heat, or cold
context: Pets suffer in heat and cold like people do; during an outage they need shade or warmth, water, and their food and medicines. Also called dog in heat, pets cold weather, pets during outage. Look for heavy panting, drooling, or weakness in heat; shivering or lethargy in cold. Keep pets indoors with you, give plenty of water, never leave them in a parked car, and bring them when you go to a warming or cooling center that accepts pets.

title: Helping children after a hard event
context: After a close call, a death, or seeing an animal harvested, children need brief, age-appropriate words, honest answers, and permission to have feelings. Also called kid saw something scary, child grief, explaining death to child, child after hunting harvest. Look for questions, drawings, or play about the event; clinginess or nightmares. Answer simply and honestly, keep routines, and let them talk or not; tell them it is okay to feel sad or confused.

title: Youth seasons and mentored hunts
context: Many states have youth days or apprentice licenses with special rules on age, supervision, and hunter education; they change by year. Also called youth deer season, kids hunting license, apprentice license. Look for the state's minimum age and supervision distance; a hunter-education course requirement. Read your state agency's current youth-hunting page and follow its supervision rules.

title: Supporting a teenager in crisis
context: A teenager in crisis needs an adult who listens calmly, takes their words seriously, and connects them with help. Also called teen depressed, teenager suicidal, help my teen. Look for withdrawal, giving things away, or talk of death; sudden changes in sleep, school, or friends. Listen without judging, ask directly about suicide if worried, lock up guns and medicines, and call or text 988 together.

title: Emergency contact and medical card
context: A small paper card with emergency contacts, allergies, medicines, and conditions helps responders when a phone is locked or dead. Also called medical info card, emergency contacts on paper, ICE contact. Look for names and numbers of two contacts; allergies, medicines, and conditions. Make a card for each family member, update it when medicines change, and add emergency contacts to your phone's lock-screen medical info.

title: Checking on older relatives and neighbors
context: Older adults are at higher risk in heat, cold, and outages, especially if they live alone or rely on medical devices. Also called check on elderly parent, older neighbor heat, senior in power outage. Look for no answer by phone during an outage or heat wave; confusion, weakness, or a cold or hot home. Call or visit twice a day during extreme weather or outages, help them reach a cooling or warming center, and make sure they have water and medicines.

title: Children and water
context: Drowning is quick and silent; children need a watcher whose eyes stay on them and a life jacket near open water. Also called kids drowning, child near pond, life jacket kids, swimming safety kids. Look for a designated adult watcher with no phone; a properly fitted life jacket. Name one adult watcher at a time, keep young children within arm's reach, and use life jackets on boats and near rivers and ponds.
